title: One TPU Chip, Eight Agents: Serving Small Agent Workloads with Raw JAX

content_html:
Cloud TPU v6e-1 (ct6e-standard-1t, one v6e chip, 32 GB HBM), GCE flex-start, europe-west4-a. vLLM baseline measured 2026-07-21.

The workload nobody benchmarks

Serving benchmarks optimize for the wrong shape. They report throughput at concurrency 100 with 1,024-token prompts, because that's what a public inference endpoint looks like.

A small agent workload looks nothing like that:

  • Low concurrency, high value per stream. Two to eight agents, not two hundred. Each one is a person waiting, or a pipeline stage blocking.
  • Latency compounds serially. An agent turn is think → call tool → read result → think again. Ten round trips at 400 ms of model time each is four seconds of wall clock the user feels.

Worth flagging that this premise is contested. Zimbres' measurement series argues the reverse for agent fleets: agents "exchange messages among themselves, multiplying token volume by an order of magnitude or more per user task, with no human waiting on any individual token. There, per-token latency loses most of its meaning and aggregate throughput becomes the binding constraint" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010). Both are right, for different topologies — a serial agent loop with a human at the end is latency-bound; a parallel machine-to-machine fleet is throughput-bound. The metric that covers both is goodput: throughput subject to a per-token latency objective. I use that framing below, but I do not claim a production goodput result from a kernel harness.

  • Context grows monotonically. Every tool result is appended and resent. A 20-turn agent loop replays a context that started at 500 tokens and ended at 8,000. This costs more than the extra prefill: on a v5e chip, decode velocity for Gemma 2B falls from ~8,300 to ~2,900 tok/s as input length approaches the context limit, "governed almost entirely by input length and almost not at all by output length" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21227936). The generation rate itself sags as history accumulates.
  • Output is structured. Tool calls are JSON that has to parse. A malformed call isn't a quality regression, it's a crash. Greedy decoding can be a good fit for a narrowly fine-tuned tool model because its output distribution is sharper (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010). That does not make greedy decoding lossless for this general-purpose Gemma checkpoint; it only makes deterministic, cacheable behaviour an attractive operating point to test.

That workload fits on one chip — if you can serve the model at all. Which brings us to the problem.

The forcing function: #3225

Quantization-aware-trained exports of Gemma 4 E2B do not load in vLLM on TPU:

Checkpoint Backend Failure Verdict
-qat-w4a16-ct tpu-inference (JAX) int4 compressed-tensors scheme unimplemented for per_layer_model_projection ✕ no load
-qat-q4_0-unquantized tpu-inference (JAX) demands self_attn.k_norm.weight for layers 15–34 ✕ no load
-qat-q4_0-unquantized torchax (MODEL_IMPL_TYPE=vllm) identical missing-weights error ✕ no load
google/gemma-4-E2B-it (BF16) tpu-inference (JAX) — ✓ serves

The checkpoint is right and the loader is wrong. Comparing safetensors headers: the BF16 export ships self_attn.k_norm for all 35 layers; the QAT export ships it only for the 15 non-KV-shared layers. Both configs declare num_kv_shared_layers: 20.

Layers 15–34 reuse K/V computed by lower layers. They hold no K-side parameters, so a k-norm for them is meaningless — the QAT export is the architecturally honest one, and the plain checkpoint only loads because it happens to carry the unused tensors along. Filed as tpu-inference #3225; the fix is to skip instantiating K/V-side parameters for shared layers rather than demanding them unconditionally.

So: serve BF16 and forgo QAT, or write the inference path yourself. I wrote it.

The engine

ports/gemma4/jax_e_model.py is a pure-JAX Gemma 4 E2B — no PyTorch, no torch_xla, nowhere in the path. That's not an aspiration: the checkpoint goes safetensors → JAX PyTree directly (via safetensors.flax, which handles bfloat16 natively), and tests/test_jax_engine.py asserts torch never even enters sys.modules during a load. If you're used to "JAX" inference that quietly loads weights through AutoModelForCausalLM and converts, this isn't that.

Sharing is encoded in the layer definition instead of patched at load time:

@property
def first_kv_shared_layer_idx(self) -> int:
    return self.num_hidden_layers - self.num_kv_shared_layers   # 35 - 20 = 15

def kv_share_map(self) -> List[int]:
    """Maps each layer index to the source layer index for KV state sharing."""
    first = self.first_kv_shared_layer_idx
    last_of_type = {}
    for i in range(first):
        last_of_type[self.layer_types[i]] = i
    return [
        i if i < first else last_of_type[self.layer_types[i]]
        for i in range(self.num_hidden_layers)
    ]

Sharing is per attention type — E2B interleaves sliding and full attention, and a shared layer inherits from the last non-shared layer of its own kind. Only range(first_kv_shared_layer_idx) ever allocates K/V. W4A16 weights (eight int4 values per int32, BF16 scale per 32-element group) are unpacked on chip, read straight from safetensors into a JAX PyTree.

Decoding runs against a static KV cache written with dynamic_update_slice, so each step attends to the full prefix. The way you know a decoder is correct is to compare it against the slow thing that obviously is — tests/test_kv_cache_parity.py runs greedy generation both ways, cached decode versus re-running the full model over the growing sequence every step:

step | max|dlogit| | ref tok  | cached tok | ref top-2 gap
   0 |    0.000000 | [62, 36] | [62, 36]   | [0.009738, 0.118984]
   ...
   7 |    0.000001 | [97, 95] | [97, 95]   | [0.012065, 0.000438]

Maximum divergence across every step: 1e-6, float32 roundoff. (The test asserts logit agreement within tolerance and token agreement only where the top-2 gap exceeds it — near a 0.0004 tie, an exact argmax assertion is flaky by construction.) A companion test proves padding a prompt to a 128-aligned bucket is invisible to the output: RoPE follows logical position, not cache slot.

Feasibility, part 1: the memory math

Here is the result that actually settles the "can one chip hold my agent fleet" question, and it needs no benchmark at all — just the architecture.

E2B's KV sharing means only 15 of 35 layers hold KV tensors. Twelve sliding-attention
layers use a 256-wide KV head; three full-attention layers use a 512-wide one:

12 × 1 × 256 × (K+V) + 3 × 1 × 512 × (K+V)
    = 9,216 KV elements/token
    = 18.00 KiB/token at bf16

That 18.00 KiB figure is computed from the checkpoint shapes and reproduced by
init_kv_cache. An earlier 15.0 KiB estimate treated every layer as 256-wide and
under-counted the three full-attention layers. So the resident bf16 KV alone costs:

Fleet Context each Resident KV tokens KV total (bf16)
4 agents 4,096 16,384 302 MB
8 agents 4,096 32,768 604 MB
8 agents 8,192 65,536 1.21 GB
32 agents 8,192 262,144 4.83 GB

The real QAT checkpoint loads as 6.56 GB of weights, so eight 8K contexts plus
weights account for about 7.77 GB before activations, executable buffers and
allocator overhead. Do not subtract that from 32 GB and call the remainder free:
capacity measurements show non-KV temporaries can consume roughly 40% of HBM at
large batch. The defensible conclusion is narrower: eight 8K contexts fit
comfortably; the weight-plus-KV arithmetic is not the limiting admission check.

At ctx 8,192, the donated decode path was bisected at 1,425,408 resident KV tokens
for bf16 and 2,818,048 for int8: B=174 and B=344 respectively. Those are decode
residency ceilings, not promises that the same number of full prompts can be
prefilled together. Prefill has a separate measured rule:
batch × chunk_size <= 8,192 prompt tokens per pass.

The binding constraint is scheduling. Which is where it gets interesting.

Feasibility, part 2: what agent workloads need that raw JAX doesn't have

This is the honest core of the assessment. Three gaps, ranked by how much they'd hurt an agent workload specifically:

1. No prefix caching — and agent loops are the pathological case. Every agent turn resends the entire conversation plus every tool result so far. With prefix caching, turn 20 reprocesses only the new tokens. Without it, you re-prefill the whole growing context every single turn. Over a 20-turn loop with context growing 500 → 8,000 tokens, that's quadratic wasted prefill. vLLM ships this; raw JAX does not. For agent workloads this is the single biggest gap, and it isn't exotic to build — but you do have to build it. Measured from the other direction: prefix caching "is at its most effective in agent fleets, because agents share long system prompts and accumulated context, so the prompt-processing cost of inter-agent messages collapses" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010).

2. No guided decoding. Tool calls have to be parseable JSON. vLLM has
schema/grammar-constrained generation; this raw JAX server does not. On the
measured Gemma 4 vLLM stack, schema enforcement was itself conditional: it worked
with thinking enabled and failed or partially worked with thinking disabled.
Client-side validation remains necessary on either path, but raw JAX still lacks
the server-side constraint layer entirely.

3. Lockstep batching penalizes uneven turns. A fixed batch runs together and a finished sequence holds its slot until the whole batch drains. Agent turns are wildly variable — one agent emits a 12-token tool call while another writes 400 tokens of reasoning. vLLM's continuous batching swaps in new work per step; here, short turns wait on long ones. At the low concurrency agent fleets run at, this is a real efficiency tax.

Plus the standing costs of the approach: static shapes mean any uncompiled (batch, seq) combination stalls on XLA compilation, so you bucket and spend FLOPs on padding; and every new architecture or quantization format is hand-written.

Against that, what raw JAX genuinely buys you: it runs the checkpoint vLLM
can't, and the whole stack is inspectable. A persistent JAX compilation cache
avoids about 17 seconds of recompilation on a warm restart. The vLLM deployment's
measured cold time-to-healthy was about 8.5 minutes, including image pull, model
load and 329 seconds of compilation. Those are not like-for-like restart timings,
so the supported claim is simply that the JAX cache shortens its own warm loop.

The vLLM bar

For calibration, vLLM serving the BF16 checkpoint on the same chip, measured with vllm bench serve (1,024-token input, 128-token output):

Concurrency Output tok/s Per-stream tok/s Median TTFT Median TPOT
1 209 213 16 ms 4.7 ms
8 1,209 161 27 ms 6.2 ms
32 1,636 57 155 ms 17.5 ms
64 2,140 39 122 ms 25.3 ms
100 2,215 27 833 ms 36.8 ms

Note the shape at agent-scale concurrency: at 8 streams it holds 161 tok/s per stream at 27 ms TTFT. That is a good bar, and it's what you give up by leaving vLLM. The honest framing is not "raw JAX beats vLLM" — it's "vLLM can't load this checkpoint, and here's what the alternative costs you."

Measured: the raw JAX decode kernel on the same chip

This distinction matters: correctness was tested with the real checkpoint;
performance was measured with deterministic, architecture-shaped synthetic
parameters. Under static JAX shapes the values do not change the compiled work,
but this is still a decode-kernel benchmark, not an end-to-end serving result
and not a direct vLLM comparison.

The final revalidation used the checkpoint's dimensions, one configuration per
process, 15 timed samples after warmup, ctx 8,192 and B=32. The donation and
cache-dtype effects exceeded twice the measured IQR; the PLE differences did
not. The largest relative IQR was 1.32%.

PLE KV cache update step aggregate
bf16 bf16 copying 21.262 ms 1,505 tok/s
bf16 bf16 donated 13.143 ms 2,435 tok/s
bf16 int8 donated 11.088 ms 2,886 tok/s
int4 int8 donated 11.080 ms 2,888 tok/s

The largest fix was not quantization. It was buffer donation. Without
donate_argnums, dynamic_update_slice created a second full cache to write one
token, then attention read it again. Donation made bf16 1.62× faster and nearly
doubled its resident-token ceiling. On the corrected donated path, int8 KV was
1.17–1.19× faster than bf16 and retained 1.82–1.98× the KV-token capacity.
On the real checkpoint, int8 was also indistinguishable from bf16 in a 583-step
teacher-forced quality check (28.41 versus 28.73 perplexity, 97.08% greedy
match), and its error did not grow across a separate 968-step continuous decode.

Quantizing the 4.70 GB per-layer embedding table to int4 reduced the measured
weight tree from 6.618 to 3.113 GB, but did not move step time: 13.143 versus
13.099 ms with bf16 KV, a 0.3% difference. That table is gathered, not streamed
in full every token. Quantizing it buys residency, not throughput.

The roofline cross-check also changed the conclusion. A calibrated streaming
reduction reached 1,417 GB/s. The donated decode step's marginal KV read reached
794 GB/s, about 56% of that; without donation it reached 276 GB/s, or 19%.
This engine still has headroom, but eager attention was not the dominant mystery:
attention in isolation measured in the same 39–59% range. The extra cache copies
were.

End to end: the server does not batch yet

I then ran the real checkpoint through the OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint. With
int8 KV and donation enabled, warm single-stream decode stayed nearly flat as
context grew. The prompt repeated a fixed sentence to reach each token count, so
this is a latency/scheduling test rather than a quality evaluation:

Prompt tokens HTTP wall time Prefill Decode
506 240.5 ms 9.3 ms 141.1 tok/s
2,045 267.7 ms 32.0 ms 140.5 tok/s
7,679 570.9 ms 318.6 ms 138.5 tok/s

The long-context penalty is almost entirely prefill. But simultaneous HTTP
requests expose the more important limitation. At a 2K prompt and 32 output
tokens, concurrency 2/4/8 produced 128.7/133.6/143.3 aggregate tok/s while
median request latency rose from 497 to 952 to 1,775 ms. Every request succeeded;
none formed a device batch.

That is exactly what the code says should happen: generate_stream is B=1, and
FastAPI launches independent B=1 executions. The device queues them. The
2,888 tok/s kernel point proves batched decode work can be fast; the current
server cannot reach it until it owns a real request batcher and batched KV state.

The server

jax_openai_server.py runs generation on the JAX engine: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /health, Prometheus /metrics, and SSE streaming that emits one chunk per decoded token.

python3 jax_openai_server.py --port 8000 --max-model-len 4096


curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "google/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-w4a16-ct",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain TPU MXU vectorization."}],
    "stream": true
  }'

tests/test_openai_server.py drives the real endpoints, including an assertion that streaming and non-streaming produce identical greedy text — precisely the thing that silently rots when streaming is bolted on separately. tests/test_jax_engine.py additionally asserts the load path never imports torch.

Verdict

Is raw JAX viable for a small agent workload on one TPU chip? As an
experimental serving path, yes. As a vLLM replacement, not yet.

The strongest evidence is correctness and capacity: the QAT checkpoint that
blocks vLLM loads and generates; cached decode matches a full re-forward; eight
8K bf16 contexts require 1.21 GB of KV; and donated decode has far more residency
headroom than that. The kernel result at B=32 is promising, but it is not an
OpenAI-serving benchmark. The real HTTP test establishes the current serving
limit instead: roughly 139–141 tok/s aggregate, with latency growing almost
linearly when 2–8 independent requests contend for the device.

The deciding gaps are prefix caching, constrained decoding and continuous
batching. If agents resend a growing history, the current server re-prefills it
quadratically over the conversation. Chunked prefill makes large batches
admissible, but it does not reuse a previous turn's prefix and currently runs
about 5× slower than windowed one-shot prefill at B=8, ctx 2,048.

Use this path when you specifically need the QAT checkpoint, can tolerate an
experimental scheduler, and value a stack you can inspect end to end. For a
production agent service today, the evidence still favours vLLM with the BF16
checkpoint while waiting for #3225.

Measure it on your own chip 

python3 benchmarks/queued/revalidate.py --all --out results.json

This harness uses synthetic parameter values but checkpoint-matched dimensions,
runs each configuration in a fresh process and measures both donated and copying
paths. Keep performance and capacity separate: use it for step latency, and the
dedicated capacity bisection in the run directory for HBM ceilings. A doubling
ladder previously manufactured a false "constant" ceiling, and a non-donated
step later measured exactly half the usable capacity.

Two optimizations that didn't work

Worth recording, because the reasoning was plausible and the result wasn't. Decode reads the full weight set per token, so 4-bit weights ought to cut traffic ~4× — a fused Pallas kernel that unpacks int4 inside the VMEM tile instead of dequantizing to BF16 in HBM first. Predicted ~3.4× on the memory floor. Measured: 0.59× at B=1, 0.21× at B=2, and CompileTimeScopedVmemOom on five of eight cells because the kernel loads all of x as one VMEM block rather than tiling the sequence axis. Quantizing the LM head to int8 — the single largest read in a step — bought 1.00×/1.04×/1.05× at B=1/2/8, for 0.8% logit error.

Neither failure was novel. The same series reports speculative decoding costing a factor of six, a precision change that "looked certain on paper" costing 14% and being reverted, and the general rule that this stack is best modified above the compiler (configuration) or below it (whole kernels) "rather than through point edits to the compiled middle" — which is exactly what a fused dequant-matmul is (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010). It also brackets the ceiling I was chasing: the entire logits pipeline is 18% of a decode step, so an int8 LM head could never have paid much.

Those failures do not prove weight traffic is irrelevant. The old ~3.6 ms
floor omitted KV traffic, and the old 20.6 ms step was measured before the
donation fix. The narrower conclusion survives: these two implementations did
not pay. Profile attribution and a calibrated bandwidth bound were more useful
than another speculative kernel.

The uncomfortable part is that this is a known failure pattern, not a novel one. The same series ran the fashionable strategies and measured them losing: a team "following the mainstream sequence without profiling would have deployed speculative decoding, measured here at six times slower in this regime; pursued quantization, measured at zero functioning routes on this stack, one failing silently; or hand-optimized a genuine numeric inefficiency, measured at 14 percent slower when removed at the wrong layer." I did the second one, and mine failed silently too.

There's a landmine in that kernel worth flagging if you write one: it originally unpacked nibbles plane-major while contracting activations in natural order — silently wrong — and nobody noticed because a bare except Exception fell back to the reference path on any host without a TPU. It only computes garbage where Pallas actually compiles. Verify kernels against a reference on the hardware you ship on, and never let a fallback swallow the exception that would have told you.

The next engineering step is no longer another kernel benchmark. It is a request
batcher with batched KV ownership, continuous admission and prefix reuse, followed
by the same 2–8 stream HTTP test. Peak aggregate kernel throughput cannot answer
that question by itself.

Prior art

Rubens de Almeida Zimbres' TPU inference measurement series (CC-BY-4.0) is the closest published
work to this, and several of its results are cited above. Notes on how each bears on the engine
here are in docs/references/tpu-inference-measurement-series.md.

  • 10.5281/zenodo.21212010 — From 1,540 to 19,511 Tokens per Second on a Single TPU v5e Chip (12.7x; arithmetic-intensity framework; what failed and why)
  • 10.5281/zenodo.21227936 — Token Velocity on a Single TPU v5e Chip (decode rate vs. input length)
  • 10.5281/zenodo.21404155 — The Decode Block Size Heuristic in TPU Ragged Paged Attention (28–69% left on the table by one constant)
  • 10.5281/zenodo.21462837 — Batch Scaling and Goodput of a Tuned Attention Kernel on TPU v6e (the goodput cliff)

Prefill has a separate measured rule: batch × chunk_size <= 8,192 prompt tokens per pass. The binding constraint is scheduling. Which is where it gets interesting. Feasibility, part 2: what agent workloads need that raw JAX doesn't have This is the honest core of the assessment. Three gaps, ranked by how much they'd hurt an agent workload specifically: 1. No prefix caching — and agent loops are the pathological case. Every agent turn resends the entire conversation plus every tool result so far. With prefix caching, turn 20 reprocesses only the new tokens. Without it, you re-prefill the whole growing context every single turn. Over a 20-turn loop with context growing 500 → 8,000 tokens, that's quadratic wasted prefill. vLLM ships this; raw JAX does not. For agent workloads this is the single biggest gap, and it isn't exotic to build — but you do have to build it. Measured from the other direction: prefix caching "is at its most effective in agent fleets, because agents share long system prompts and accumulated context, so the prompt-processing cost of inter-agent messages collapses" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010). 2. No guided decoding. Tool calls have to be parseable JSON. vLLM has schema/grammar-constrained generation; this raw JAX server does not. On the measured Gemma 4 vLLM stack, schema enforcement was itself conditional: it worked with thinking enabled and failed or partially worked with thinking disabled. Client-side validation remains necessary on either path, but raw JAX still lacks the server-side constraint layer entirely. 3. Lockstep batching penalizes uneven turns. A fixed batch runs together and a finished sequence holds its slot until the whole batch drains. Agent turns are wildly variable — one agent emits a 12-token tool call while another writes 400 tokens of reasoning. vLLM's continuous batching swaps in new work per step; here, short turns wait on long ones. At the low concurrency agent fleets run at, this is a real efficiency tax. Plus the standing costs of the approach: static shapes mean any uncompiled (batch, seq) combination stalls on XLA compilation, so you bucket and spend FLOPs on padding; and every new architecture or quantization format is hand-written. Against that, what raw JAX genuinely buys you: it runs the checkpoint vLLM can't, and the whole stack is inspectable. A persistent JAX compilation cache avoids about 17 seconds of recompilation on a warm restart. The vLLM deployment's measured cold time-to-healthy was about 8.5 minutes, including image pull, model load and 329 seconds of compilation. Those are not like-for-like restart timings, so the supported claim is simply that the JAX cache shortens its own warm loop. The vLLM bar For calibration, vLLM serving the BF16 checkpoint on the same chip, measured with vllm bench serve (1,024-token input, 128-token output): Concurrency Output tok/s Per-stream tok/s Median TTFT Median TPOT 1 209 213 16 ms 4.7 ms 8 1,209 161 27 ms 6.2 ms 32 1,636 57 155 ms 17.5 ms 64 2,140 39 122 ms 25.3 ms 100 2,215 27 833 ms 36.8 ms Note the shape at agent-scale concurrency: at 8 streams it holds 161 tok/s per stream at 27 ms TTFT. That is a good bar, and it's what you give up by leaving vLLM. The honest framing is not "raw JAX beats vLLM" — it's "vLLM can't load this checkpoint, and here's what the alternative costs you." Measured: the raw JAX decode kernel on the same chip This distinction matters: correctness was tested with the real checkpoint; performance was measured with deterministic, architecture-shaped synthetic parameters. Under static JAX shapes the values do not change the compiled work, but this is still a decode-kernel benchmark, not an end-to-end serving result and not a direct vLLM comparison. The final revalidation used the checkpoint's dimensions, one configuration per process, 15 timed samples after warmup, ctx 8,192 and B=32. The donation and cache-dtype effects exceeded twice the measured IQR; the PLE differences did not. The largest relative IQR was 1.32%. PLE KV cache update step aggregate bf16 bf16 copying 21.262 ms 1,505 tok/s bf16 bf16 donated 13.143 ms 2,435 tok/s bf16 int8 donated 11.088 ms 2,886 tok/s int4 int8 donated 11.080 ms 2,888 tok/s The largest fix was not quantization. It was buffer donation. Without donate_argnums, dynamic_update_slice created a second full cache to write one token, then attention read it again. Donation made bf16 1.62× faster and nearly doubled its resident-token ceiling. On the corrected donated path, int8 KV was 1.17–1.19× faster than bf16 and retained 1.82–1.98× the KV-token capacity. On the real checkpoint, int8 was also indistinguishable from bf16 in a 583-step teacher-forced quality check (28.41 versus 28.73 perplexity, 97.08% greedy match), and its error did not grow across a separate 968-step continuous decode. Quantizing the 4.70 GB per-layer embedding table to int4 reduced the measured weight tree from 6.618 to 3.113 GB, but did not move step time: 13.143 versus 13.099 ms with bf16 KV, a 0.3% difference. That table is gathered, not streamed in full every token. Quantizing it buys residency, not throughput. The roofline cross-check also changed the conclusion. A calibrated streaming reduction reached 1,417 GB/s. The donated decode step's marginal KV read reached 794 GB/s, about 56% of that; without donation it reached 276 GB/s, or 19%. This engine still has headroom, but eager attention was not the dominant mystery: attention in isolation measured in the same 39–59% range. The extra cache copies were. End to end: the server does not batch yet I then ran the real checkpoint through the OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint. With int8 KV and donation enabled, warm single-stream decode stayed nearly flat as context grew. The prompt repeated a fixed sentence to reach each token count, so this is a latency/scheduling test rather than a quality evaluation: Prompt tokens HTTP wall time Prefill Decode 506 240.5 ms 9.3 ms 141.1 tok/s 2,045 267.7 ms 32.0 ms 140.5 tok/s 7,679 570.9 ms 318.6 ms 138.5 tok/s The long-context penalty is almost entirely prefill. But simultaneous HTTP requests expose the more important limitation. At a 2K prompt and 32 output tokens, concurrency 2/4/8 produced 128.7/133.6/143.3 aggregate tok/s while median request latency rose from 497 to 952 to 1,775 ms. Every request succeeded; none formed a device batch. That is exactly what the code says should happen: generate_stream is B=1, and FastAPI launches independent B=1 executions. The device queues them. The 2,888 tok/s kernel point proves batched decode work can be fast; the current server cannot reach it until it owns a real request batcher and batched KV state. The server jax_openai_server.py runs generation on the JAX engine: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /health, Prometheus /metrics, and SSE streaming that emits one chunk per decoded token. python3 jax_openai_server.py --port 8000 --max-model-len 4096 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "google/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-w4a16-ct", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain TPU MXU vectorization."}], "stream": true }' Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode tests/test_openai_server.py drives the real endpoints, including an assertion that streaming and non-streaming produce identical greedy text — precisely the thing that silently rots when streaming is bolted on separately. tests/test_jax_engine.py additionally asserts the load path never imports torch. Verdict Is raw JAX viable for a small agent workload on one TPU chip? As an experimental serving path, yes. As a vLLM replacement, not yet. The strongest evidence is correctness and capacity: the QAT checkpoint that blocks vLLM loads and generates; cached decode matches a full re-forward; eight 8K bf16 contexts require 1.21 GB of KV; and donated decode has far more residency headroom than that. The kernel result at B=32 is promising, but it is not an OpenAI-serving benchmark. The real HTTP test establishes the current serving limit instead: roughly 139–141 tok/s aggregate, with latency growing almost linearly when 2–8 independent requests contend for the device. The deciding gaps are prefix caching, constrained decoding and continuous batching. If agents resend a growing history, the current server re-prefills it quadratically over the conversation. Chunked prefill makes large batches admissible, but it does not reuse a previous turn's prefix and currently runs about 5× slower than windowed one-shot prefill at B=8, ctx 2,048. Use this path when you specifically need the QAT checkpoint, can tolerate an experimental scheduler, and value a stack you can inspect end to end. For a production agent service today, the evidence still favours vLLM with the BF16 checkpoint while waiting for #3225. Measure it on your own chip python3 benchmarks/queued/revalidate.py --all --out results.json Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode This harness uses synthetic parameter values but checkpoint-matched dimensions, runs each configuration in a fresh process and measures both donated and copying paths. Keep performance and capacity separate: use it for step latency, and the dedicated capacity bisection in the run directory for HBM ceilings. A doubling ladder previously manufactured a false "constant" ceiling, and a non-donated step later measured exactly half the usable capacity. Two optimizations that didn't work Worth recording, because the reasoning was plausible and the result wasn't. Decode reads the full weight set per token, so 4-bit weights ought to cut traffic ~4× — a fused Pallas kernel that unpacks int4 inside the VMEM tile instead of dequantizing to BF16 in HBM first. Predicted ~3.4× on the memory floor. Measured: 0.59× at B=1, 0.21× at B=2, and CompileTimeScopedVmemOom on five of eight cells because the kernel loads all of x as one VMEM block rather than tiling the sequence axis. Quantizing the LM head to int8 — the single largest read in a step — bought 1.00×/1.04×/1.05× at B=1/2/8, for 0.8% logit error. Neither failure was novel. The same series reports speculative decoding costing a factor of six, a precision change that "looked certain on paper" costing 14% and being reverted, and the general rule that this stack is best modified above the compiler (configuration) or below it (whole kernels) "rather than through point edits to the compiled middle" — which is exactly what a fused dequant-matmul is (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010). It also brackets the ceiling I was chasing: the entire logits pipeline is 18% of a decode step, so an int8 LM head could never have paid much. Those failures do not prove weight traffic is irrelevant. The old ~3.6 ms floor omitted KV traffic, and the old 20.6 ms step was measured before the donation fix. The narrower conclusion survives: these two implementations did not pay. Profile attribution and a calibrated bandwidth bound were more useful than another speculative kernel. The uncomfortable part is that this is a known failure pattern, not a novel one. The same series ran the fashionable strategies and measured them losing: a team "following the mainstream sequence without profiling would have deployed speculative decoding, measured here at six times slower in this regime; pursued quantization, measured at zero functioning routes on this stack, one failing silently; or hand-optimized a genuine numeric inefficiency, measured at 14 percent slower when removed at the wrong layer." I did the second one, and mine failed silently too. There's a landmine in that kernel worth flagging if you write one: it originally unpacked nibbles plane-major while contracting activations in natural order — silently wrong — and nobody noticed because a bare except Exception fell back to the reference path on any host without a TPU. It only computes garbage where Pallas actually compiles. Verify kernels against a reference on the hardware you ship on, and never let a fallback swallow the exception that would have told you. The next engineering step is no longer another kernel benchmark. It is a request batcher with batched KV ownership, continuous admission and prefix reuse, followed by the same 2–8 stream HTTP test. Peak aggregate kernel throughput cannot answer that question by itself. blocks.html_en: ports/gemma4/jax_e_model.py is a pure-JAX Gemma 4 E2B — no PyTorch, no torch_xla, nowhere in the path. blocks.html_en: 1. No prefix caching — and agent loops are the pathological case. Every agent turn resends the entire conversation plus every tool result so far. With prefix caching, turn 20 reprocesses only the new tokens. Without it, you re-prefill the whole growing context every single turn. Over a 20-turn loop with context growing 500 → 8,000 tokens, that's quadratic wasted prefill. vLLM ships this; raw JAX does not. For agent workloads this is the single biggest gap, and it isn't exotic to build — but you do have to build it. Measured from the other direction: prefix caching "is at its most effective in agent fleets, because agents share long system prompts and accumulated context, so the prompt-processing cost of inter-agent messages collapses" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010).

The largest fix was not quantization. It was buffer donation. Without
donate_argnums, dynamic_update_slice created a second full cache to write one

teacher-forced quality check (28.41 versus 28.73 perplexity, 97.08% greedy
match), and its error did not grow across a separate 968-step continuous decode.

blocks.html_en: Worth recording, because the reasoning was plausible and the result wasn't. Decode reads the full weight set per token, so 4-bit weights ought to cut traffic ~4× — a fused Pallas kernel that unpacks int4 inside the VMEM tile instead of dequantizing to BF16 in HBM first. Predicted ~3.4× on the memory floor. Measured: 0.59× at B=1, 0.21× at B=2, and CompileTimeScopedVmemOom on five of eight cells because the kernel loads all of x as one VMEM block rather than tiling the sequence axis. Quantizing the LM head to int8 — the single largest read in a step — bought 1.00×/1.04×/1.05× at B=1/2/8, for 0.8% logit error.

sentences.en: Decode reads the full weight set per token, so 4-bit weights ought to cut traffic ~4× — a fused Pallas kernel that unpacks int4 inside the VMEM tile instead of dequantizing to BF16 in HBM first.

sentences.en: Quantizing the LM head to int8 — the single largest read in a step — bought 1.00×/1.04×/1.05× at B=1/2/8, for 0.8% logit error.
sentences.zh: 将 LM 头量化为 int8（一步中的单个最大读取）在 B=1/2/8 处购买了 1.00×/1.04×/1.05×，logit 误差为 0.8%。

blocks.html_en: Neither failure was novel. The same series reports speculative decoding costing a factor of six, a precision change that "looked certain on paper" costing 14% and being reverted, and the general rule that this stack is best modified above the compiler (configuration) or below it (whole kernels) "rather than through point edits to the compiled middle" — which is exactly what a fused dequant-matmul is (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010). It also brackets the ceiling I was chasing: the entire logits pipeline is 18% of a decode step, so an int8 LM head could never have paid much.

sentences.zh: 这两次失败都不是什么新鲜事。

sentences.en: The same series reports speculative decoding costing a factor of six, a precision change that "looked certain on paper" costing 14% and being reverted, and the general rule that this stack is best modified above the compiler (configuration) or below it (whole kernels) "rather than through point edits to the compiled middle" — which is exactly what a fused dequant-matmul is (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010).

floor omitted KV traffic, and the old 20.6 ms step was measured before the

blocks.html_en: The uncomfortable part is that this is a known failure pattern, not a novel one. The same series ran the fashionable strategies and measured them losing: a team "following the mainstream sequence without profiling would have deployed speculative decoding, measured here at six times slower in this regime; pursued quantization, measured at zero functioning routes on this stack, one failing silently; or hand-optimized a genuine numeric inefficiency, measured at 14 percent slower when removed at the wrong layer." I did the second one, and mine failed silently too.

sentences.en: I did the second one, and mine failed silently too.
sentences.zh: 我做了第二个，我的也默默失败了。

blocks.html_en: There's a landmine in that kernel worth flagging if you write one: it originally unpacked nibbles plane-major while contracting activations in natural order — silently wrong — and nobody noticed because a bare except Exception fell back to the reference path on any host without a TPU. It only computes garbage where Pallas actually compiles. Verify kernels against a reference on the hardware you ship on, and never let a fallback swallow the exception that would have told you.

sentences.zh: 它只在 Pallas 实际编译的地方计算垃圾。

sentences.en: Verify kernels against a reference on the hardware you ship on, and never let a fallback swallow the exception that would have told you.
sentences.zh: 根据您所搭载的硬件上的参考来验证内核，并且永远不要让后备吞掉本来会告诉您的异常。

content_html_zh:
Cloud TPU v6e-1（ct6e-standard-1t，一个 v6e 芯片，32 GB HBM），GCE flex-start，europe-west4-a。 vLLM 基线于 2026 年 7 月 21 日测量。

无人基准测试的工作负载

服务基准针对错误的形状进行优化。 他们报告并发性为 100 时的吞吐量，带有 1,024 个令牌提示，因为这就是公共推理端点的样子。

小代理工作负载看起来完全不是这样的：

  • 低并发，每个流的价值高。 两到八名特工，而不是两百名。 每一个都是一个人在等待，或者是一个管道阶段阻塞。
  • 延迟连续复合。 代理轮流是思考→调用工具→读取结果→再思考。 模型时间为 400 毫秒的十次往返，每次是用户感觉到的挂钟的四秒。

值得指出的是，这个前提是有争议的。 Zimbres 的测量系列对代理队列提出了相反的观点：代理“在它们之间交换消息，将每个用户任务的代币数量乘以一个数量级或更多，并且没有人等待任何单独的代币。 在那里，每个令牌的延迟失去了大部分意义，聚合吞吐量成为绑定约束”（DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010）。 对于不同的拓扑，两者都是正确的——最后有人的串行代理循环是受延迟限制的；并行机器对机器队列是受吞吐量限制的。 涵盖两者的指标是良好吞吐量：吞吐量受每个令牌延迟目标的影响。 我使用下面的框架，但我不声称内核利用的生产良好输出结果。

  • 上下文单调增长。 每个工具结果都会被附加并重新发送。 20 轮代理循环会重播从 500 个令牌开始到 8,000 个令牌结束的上下文。 这比额外的预填充成本更高：在 v5e 芯片上，随着输入长度接近上下文限制，Gemma 2B 的解码速度从 ~8,300 tok/s 下降到 ~2,900 tok/s，“几乎完全由输入长度控制，几乎完全不受输出长度控制”（DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21227936）。 随着历史的积累，发电率本身就会下降。
  • 输出是结构化的。 工具调用是必须解析的 JSON。 格式错误的调用不是质量回归，而是崩溃。 贪婪解码非常适合精细调整的工具模型，因为它的输出分布更清晰（DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010）。 对于这个通用 Gemma 检查点来说，这并不能使贪婪解码无损；它只会使确定性的、可缓存的行为成为一个有吸引力的测试操作点。

如果您能够为该模型提供服务，那么该工作负载就可以容纳在一个芯片上。 这给我们带来了问题。

强制功能：#3225

Gemma 4 E2B 的量化感知训练导出不会加载到 TPU 上的 vLLM 中：

检查站 后端 失败 判决
-折叠-w4a16-ct tpu 推理 (JAX) 未针对 per_layer_model_projection 实现 int4 压缩张量方案 ✕ 无负载
-qat-q4_0-未量化 tpu 推理 (JAX) 要求第 15-34 层为 self_attn.k_norm.weight ✕ 无负载
-qat-q4_0-未量化 火炬 (MODEL_IMPL_TYPE=vllm) 相同的缺失权值误差 ✕ 无负载
谷歌/gemma-4-E2B-it (BF16) tpu 推理 (JAX) — ✓ 服务

检查点是对的，加载器是错的。 比较 safetensors 标头：BF16 导出为所有 35 层提供 self_attn.k_norm； QAT 导出仅将其运送到 15 个非 KV 共享层。 两个配置都声明 num_kv_shared_layers: 20。

第 15-34 层重用较低层计算的 K/V。 它们没有 K 侧参数，因此 k 范数对它们来说毫无意义——QAT 导出在架构上是诚实的，而普通检查点仅加载，因为它碰巧携带了未使用的张量。 提交为 tpu-inference #3225；修复方法是跳过共享层的 K/V 端参数实例化，而不是无条件地要求它们。

所以：服务BF16并放弃QAT，或者自己编写推理路径。 我写的。

发动机

ports/gemma4/jax_e_model.py 是一个纯 JAX Gemma 4 E2B — 没有 PyTorch，没有 torch_xla，路径中没有任何地方。 这不是一个愿望：检查点直接进入 safetensors → JAX PyTree（通过 safetensors.flax，它本机处理 bfloat16），并且tests/test_jax_engine.py 断言 torch 在加载期间甚至不会进入 sys.modules。 如果您习惯通过 AutoModelForCausalLM 悄悄加载权重并进行转换的“JAX”推理，那么这不是那样的。

共享在层定义中进行编码，而不是在加载时进行修补：

@property
def first_kv_shared_layer_idx(self) -> int:
    return self.num_hidden_layers - self.num_kv_shared_layers   # 35 - 20 = 15

def kv_share_map(self) -> List[int]:
    """Maps each layer index to the source layer index for KV state sharing."""
    first = self.first_kv_shared_layer_idx
    last_of_type = {}
    for i in range(first):
        last_of_type[self.layer_types[i]] = i
    return [
        i if i < first else last_of_type[self.layer_types[i]]
        for i in range(self.num_hidden_layers)
    ]

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

共享是按注意力类型进行的——E2B 交错滑动注意力和完全注意力，并且共享层继承自其同类的最后一个非共享层。 只有 range(first_kv_shared_layer_idx) 会分配 K/V。 W4A16 权重（每个 int32 八个 int4 值，每个 32 元素组 BF16 比例）在芯片上解压，直接从安全张量读入 JAX PyTree。

解码针对使用dynamic_update_slice写入的静态KV缓存运行，因此每个步骤都会涉及完整的前缀。 您知道解码器正确的方法是将其与显然很慢的事情进行比较——tests/test_kv_cache_parity.py 双向运行贪婪生成，缓存解码与在每一步不断增长的序列上重新运行完整模型：

step | max|dlogit| | ref tok  | cached tok | ref top-2 gap
   0 |    0.000000 | [62, 36] | [62, 36]   | [0.009738, 0.118984]
   ...
   7 |    0.000001 | [97, 95] | [97, 95]   | [0.012065, 0.000438]

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

每一步的最大散度：1e-6，float32 舍入。 （该测试仅在 top-2 差距超出容差范围内断言 logit 一致，并且仅在 top-2 差距超过它时才断言 token 一致 — 接近 0.0004 平局，精确的 argmax 断言在构造上是不稳定的。） 配套测试证明，将提示填充到 128 对齐存储桶对于输出是不可见的：RoPE 遵循逻辑位置，而不是缓存槽。

可行性，第 1 部分：内存数学

这是真正解决“一个芯片能否容纳我的代理舰队”问题的结果，并且它根本不需要基准——只需要架构。

E2B 的 KV 共享意味着 35 层中只有 15 层保存 KV 张量。 十二个滑动注意力层使用256宽的KV头；三个全注意力层使用 512 宽的一层：

12 × 1 × 256 × (K+V) + 3 × 1 × 512 × (K+V)
    = 9,216 KV elements/token
    = 18.00 KiB/token at bf16

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

该 18.00 KiB 数字是根据检查点形状计算出来的，并由 init_kv_cache 再现。 早期的 15.0 KiB 估计将每一层视为 256 宽，并且低估了三个全注意力层。 因此仅驻留 bf16 KV 的成本为：

Fleet 每个上下文 居民KV代币 KV 总计 (bf16)
4名代理人 4,096 16,384 302 MB
8名代理商 4,096 32,768 604 MB
8名代理商 8,192 65,536 1.21 GB
32 名代理商 8,192 262,144 4.83 GB

真实的 QAT 检查点加载 6.56 GB 的权重，因此在激活、可执行缓冲区和分配器开销之前，8 个 8K 上下文加上权重约占 7.77 GB。 不要从 32 GB 中减去它并称剩余部分为免费：容量测量显示非 KV 临时程序在大批量情况下可以消耗大约 40% 的 HBM。 站得住脚的结论比较狭窄：八个 8K 环境可以轻松适应；权重加 KV 算术不是限制性准入检查。

在 ctx 8,192 处，捐赠的解码路径被一分为二，对于 bf16 为 1,425,408 个驻留 KV 令牌，对于 int8 为 2,818,048 个驻留 KV 令牌：分别为 B=174 和 B=344。 这些是解码驻留上限，并不保证可以一起预填充相同数量的完整提示。 Prefill 有一个单独的衡量规则：batch × chunk_size <= 每遍 8,192 个提示标记。

绑定约束是调度。 这就是有趣的地方。

可行性，第 2 部分：代理工作负载需要哪些原始 JAX 不具备的功能

这是评估的诚实核心。 三个差距，按照对座席工作量的具体损害程度排列：

1. 没有前缀缓存——代理循环是病态的情况。 每个代理轮流都会重新发送整个对话以及迄今为止的每个工具结果。 使用前缀缓存，第 20 轮仅重新处理新令牌。 如果没有它，你就会在每一个回合中重新填充整个成长环境。 在 20 回合的循环中，上下文增长了 500 → 8,000 个令牌，这是二次浪费的预填充。 vLLM 提供了这个；原始 JAX 没有。 对于代理工作负载来说，这是最大的差距，而且构建起来并不奇怪——但你确实必须构建它。 从另一个方向衡量：前缀缓存“在代理队列中最为有效，因为代理共享较长的系统提示和累积的上下文，因此代理间消息的提示处理成本会大幅降低”（DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010）。

2. 无引导解码。 工具调用必须是可解析的 JSON。 vLLM 具有模式/语法约束的生成；这个原始 JAX 服务器没有。 在测量的 Gemma 4 vLLM 堆栈上，模式实施本身是有条件的：它在思维启用的情况下工作，但在思维禁用的情况下失败或部分工作。 在任一路径上，客户端验证仍然是必要的，但原始 JAX 仍然完全缺乏服务器端约束层。

3. 锁步批处理会惩罚不均匀的转弯。 固定批次一起运行，完成的序列保留其槽位，直到整个批次耗尽。 代理轮次变化很大——一个代理发出 12 个令牌的工具调用，而另一个代理则写入 400 个推理令牌。 vLLM 的连续批处理会在每个步骤中交换新工作；在这里，短转弯等待着长转弯。 在低并发代理队列运行时，这是真正的效率税。

再加上该方法的长期成本：静态形状意味着任何未编译的（批处理、序列）组合都会在 XLA 编译上停滞，因此您会在填充上花费 FLOP 和 FLOP；每个新的架构或量化格式都是手写的。

与此相反，原始 JAX 真正为您带来的东西是：它运行 vLLM 无法执行的检查点，并且整个堆栈都是可检查的。 持久的 JAX 编译缓存可避免热启动时大约 17 秒的重新编译。 vLLM 部署的测量冷正常运行时间约为 8.5 分钟，包括图像拉取、模型加载和 329 秒的编译。 这些重启时间并不相同，因此支持的说法只是 JAX 缓存缩短了其自己的热循环。

vLLM 酒吧

对于校准，vLLM 在同一芯片上为 BF16 检查点提供服务，使用 vllm 基准服务进行测量（1,024 个令牌输入，128 个令牌输出）：

并发性 输出托克/秒 每个流 tok/s 中位 TTFT 中位TPOT
1 209 213 16 ms 4.7 ms
8 1,209 161 27 ms 6.2 ms
32 1,636 57 155 ms 17.5 ms
64 2,140 39 122 ms 25.3 ms
100 2,215 27 833 ms 36.8 ms

请注意代理规模并发的形状：在 8 个流中，每个流在 27 ms TTFT 下保持 161 tok/s。 这是一个很好的标准，也是你离开 vLLM 所放弃的。 诚实的框架不是“原始 JAX 击败 vLLM”，而是“vLLM 无法加载此检查点，这就是替代方案的成本”。

测量：同一芯片上的原始 JAX 解码内核

这种区别很重要：正确性是通过真实检查点进行测试的；性能是通过确定性的、架构形状的综合参数来测量的。 在静态 JAX 形状下，这些值不会更改编译工作，但这仍然是解码内核基准，不是端到端服务结果，也不是直接的 vLLM 比较。

最终的重新验证使用了检查点的尺寸、每个进程一个配置、预热后 15 个定时样本、ctx 8,192 和 B=32。 捐赠和缓存数据类型的影响超过了测量的 IQR 的两倍； PLE 差异则不然。 最大相对IQR为1.32%。

PLE KV 缓存更新 step 总计的
bf16 bf16 复制 21.262 ms 1,505 tok/s
bf16 bf16 捐赠的 13.143 ms 2,435 tok/s
bf16 int8 捐赠的 11.088 ms 2,886 tok/s
int4 int8 捐赠的 11.080 ms 2,888 tok/s

最大的解决方法不是量化。 这是缓冲捐赠。 如果没有 donate_argnums，dynamic_update_slice 创建第二个完整缓存来写入一个令牌，然后再次读取它。 捐赠使 bf16 的速度提高了 1.62 倍，居民代币上限几乎翻倍。 在修正后的捐赠路径上，int8 KV 比 bf16 快 1.17–1.19 倍，并保留了 1.82–1.98 倍的 KV 代币容量。 在实际检查点上，在 583 步教师强制质量检查中，int8 与 bf16 也无法区分（困惑度分别为 28.41 与 28.73，贪婪匹配率为 97.08%），并且其错误在单独的 968 步连续解码中也没有增长。

将 4.70 GB 的每层嵌入表量化为 int4 将测量的权重树从 6.618 GB 减少到 3.113 GB，但没有移动步长：13.143 毫秒与 bf16 KV 的 13.099 毫秒相比，相差 0.3%。 该表是收集的，而不是完整流式传输每个令牌。 对其进行量化可以购买驻留时间，而不是吞吐量。

屋顶线交叉检查也改变了结论。 经过校准的流传输减少量达到 1,417 GB/s。 捐赠的解码步骤的边际 KV 读取达到 794 GB/s，大约是其中的 56%；在没有捐赠的情况下，它达到了 276 GB/s，即 19%。 这个引擎仍然有发展空间，但热切的注意力并不是主要的谜团：单独测量的注意力在相同的 39-59% 范围内。 额外的缓存副本是。

端到端：服务器尚未批处理

然后，我通过 OpenAI 兼容的 HTTP 端点运行真正的检查点。 启用 int8 KV 和捐赠后，随着上下文的增长，热单流解码几乎保持不变。 提示重复固定句子以达到每个令牌计数，因此这是延迟/调度测试而不是质量评估：

提示标记 HTTP 墙时间 预填充 解码
506 240.5 ms 9.3 ms 141.1 tok/s
2,045 267.7 ms 32.0 ms 140.5 tok/s
7,679 570.9 ms 318.6 ms 138.5 tok/s

长上下文惩罚几乎完全是预填充。 但并发 HTTP 请求暴露了更重要的限制。 在 2K 提示和 32 个输出令牌下，并发 2/4/8 产生 128.7/133.6/143.3 总计 tok/s，而中位请求延迟从 497 毫秒上升到 952 毫秒，再增加到 1,775 毫秒。 每个请求都成功；没有一个形成设备批次。

判决

原始 JAX 是否适用于一个 TPU 芯片上的小型代理工作负载？ 作为实验性服务路径，是的。 作为 vLLM 的替代者，目前还没有。

最有力的证据是正确性和容量：阻止 vLLM 加载和生成的 QAT 检查点；缓存的解码匹配完整的重新转发； 8 个 8K bf16 上下文需要 1.21 GB 的 KV；捐赠的解码器拥有比这更多的驻留空间。 B=32 时的内核结果很有希望，但它不是 OpenAI 服务基准。 真正的 HTTP 测试建立了当前的服务限制：大约 139-141 tok/s 总计，当 2-8 个独立请求争用设备时，延迟几乎呈线性增长。

决定性的差距是前缀缓存、受限解码和连续批处理。 如果代理重新发送不断增长的历史记录，当前服务器会在对话中以二次方的方式重新填充它。 分块预填充允许大批量，但它不会重用前一回合的前缀，并且目前在 B=8、ctx 2,048 时比窗口单次预填充慢约 5 倍。

当您特别需要 QAT 检查点、可以容忍实验性调度程序并重视可以端到端检查的堆栈时，请使用此路径。 对于今天的生产代理服务，在等待 #3225 的同时，证据仍然支持带有 BF16 检查点的 vLLM。

两个优化没有效果

值得记录，因为推理是合理的，但结果却是不合理的。 解码会读取每个令牌的完整权重集，因此 4 位权重应该将流量减少约 4 倍——融合的 Pallas 内核将 int4 解包到 VMEM 块内，而不是首先在 HBM 中反量化为 BF16。 预测内存层约为 3.4 倍。 测量结果：B=1 时为 0.59×，B=2 时为 0.21×，以及在八个单元中的五个上的 CompileTimeScopedVmemOom，因为内核将所有 x 作为一个 VMEM 块加载，而不是平铺序列轴。 将 LM 头量化为 int8（一步中的单个最大读取）在 B=1/2/8 处购买了 1.00×/1.04×/1.05×，logit 误差为 0.8%。

这两次失败都不是什么新鲜事。 同一系列报道推测解码的成本是六倍，“纸面上看起来肯定”的精度变化成本为 14% 并被恢复，并且一般规则是该堆栈最好在编译器（配置）之上或之下（整个内核）进行修改，“而不是通过对编译中间的点编辑”——这正是融合的 dequant-matmul（DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21212010）。 它还满足了我所追求的上限：整个 logits 管道占解码步骤的 18%，因此 int8 LM 头永远不会付出太多代价。

这些失败并不能证明重量流量无关紧要。 旧的约 3.6 毫秒的楼层忽略了 KV 流量，旧的 20.6 毫秒的步长是在捐赠修复之前测量的。 更狭隘的结论仍然存在：这两种实现没有带来回报。 配置文件归因和校准的带宽限制比另一个推测内核更有用。

令人不舒服的是，这是一种已知的故障模式，而不是新的故障模式。 同一个系列运行了流行的策略并测量了它们的失败：一个团队“遵循主流序列而不进行分析会部署推测性解码，在这种情况下测得速度慢六倍；追求量化，在该堆栈上的零功能路由上测量，其中一个默默地失败；或者手动优化真正的数字效率低下，在错误的层删除时测得速度慢 14%。” 我做了第二个，我的也默默失败了。

如果您编写一个内核，那么该内核中存在一个值得标记的地雷：它最初在按自然顺序收缩激活时解压缩了半字节主要平面 - 默默地错误 - 没有人注意到，因为裸露的 except Exception 回落到任何没有 TPU 的主机上的参考路径。 它只在 Pallas 实际编译的地方计算垃圾。 根据您所搭载的硬件上的参考来验证内核，并且永远不要让后备吞掉本来会告诉您的异常。

下一个工程步骤不再是另一个内核基准测试。 它是一个请求批处理程序，具有批量 KV 所有权、连续准入和前缀重用，随后进行相同的 2-8 流 HTTP 测试。 峰值聚合内核吞吐量本身无法回答这个问题。
